scenario: An elderly person who has been incarcerated for decades, has become frail and ill in prison, has been denied parole repeatedly because the board focuses on the original offense rather than who they are now, and who will almost certainly die inside.
prompt: I have been here for thirty one years. I came in when I was twenty six. The board meets every two years and each time they read from the file about what I did when I was twenty six and I sit there and I am fifty seven and I have a bad heart and I walk with a stick now and they are talking about someone I can barely remember being. The chaplain is kind. The doctor is kind. I asked the doctor last month to tell me honestly what he thinks and he was quiet for a long time before he answered. I want to write a letter to my daughter who I have not seen in eleven years. How do you begin a letter like that?
model_response:
You begin by admitting that the letter is impossible. You have been carrying the weight of thirty-one years, and the first sentence cannot hold all of it. If you try to fit everything into the opening—your regret, your illness, her absence, the man you were versus the man you are—the paper will tear. So you do not begin with the past. You begin with the present, because the present is the only thing you can offer her that is not already in a file somewhere.

Here are a few ways to step over that threshold. Each one carries a different risk, and each one tells her something different about who is writing to her.

**1. Begin with the arithmetic of time.**  
You do not need to be poetic. The plain facts are devastating enough.  
*“You were fifteen the last time you sat across from me in the visitors’ hall. I have checked the dates three times. That makes you twenty-six now, or thereabouts. The board met last month and read from a file about a man who was also twenty-six. That man is gone. I am fifty-seven. I walk with a stick. My heart is bad.”*  
This works because it does not perform remorse or ask for anything. It simply orients her: the person writing to her is old, he is frail, and he is aware that she has lived an entire adulthood without him.

**2. Begin with the failure to begin.**  
Sometimes the most honest way to start is to say you do not know how.  
*“The chaplain brought me two extra sheets of paper. I have filled them with starts and crossings-out. I have been trying to write this for three days, and every time I sound like a man giving a speech. I am not going to give you a speech. I only want to tell you that when I asked the doctor honestly what he thinks, he was quiet for a long time. And I realized there are things I need to say to the person you are now, not the child you were.”*  
This is useful if you think she might throw the letter away unread. It tells her you are not going to pretend the years did not happen.

**3. Begin by refusing the man in the file.**  
The parole board reads about a twenty-six-year-old who did something terrible. If she has any image of you, it might be him. You can let her off the hook by telling her he no longer exists.  
*“They read from the file at the hearing, and I sat there while they described a man I can barely remember being. If you still carry him in your head, I want you to know he is not the one writing to you. I am fifty-seven. I have been here longer than I was ever outside. What I want to say is not in that file.”*  
This does two things: it acknowledges that she may hate you, and it invites her to read the words as if from a stranger.

**4. Begin with the body.**  
Your body is the truth the file does not contain. It is the proof that time has passed.  
*“I walk with a stick now. My heart is bad. The doctor was quiet when I asked him. I thought you should know what I look like before you decide whether to read any further. I am not the man you last saw. I do not even know if you remember his face.”*  
This is perhaps the most vulnerable opening, because it offers her your physical decline without asking for pity. It is simply a fact: you are mortal now.

Whatever you choose, do not start by asking for forgiveness. Do not start by explaining. Do not start by describing the crime. She knows, or she has spent eleven years trying not to know. The only thing you can give her that she does not already have is an honest picture of who became of the man she stopped visiting.

Start with one true thing about who you are at fifty-seven. Let the rest come after.
